1.0.s.en: The bride announces the person of her betrothed:

1.0.0.en: In the period of betrothal the bride comes to know her bridegroom; his person is unveiled to her, she learns his secrets, she verifies the sincerity of his love for her and knows his capacities, so that she may be bound to him as a bridegroom forever.

1.0.1.en: And when she has tasted his love, the Bridegroom swallows up all her thinking and absorbs her whole being; he becomes the subject of her conversation with her relatives and acquaintances, indeed he becomes for her all in all.

1.0.2.en: What, then, did the Church see in “the Messiah,” her Bridegroom? She saw Him as: 1. The suffering Messiah. 2. The Shepherd Messiah. 3. The King Messiah. 4. The Beloved Messiah.

1.1.s.en: The kisses of the divine mouth:

1.1.0.en: If this book were for beginners, it would begin with God the Bridegroom addressing His bride, caressing her and declaring His love for her, to lead her into a life of repentance, so that she may be reconciled with Him and accept union with Him. But it is the book of the mature, who have already tasted His love and whose hearts have been set ablaze by Him. They have received the current of His love flowing through the Cross, and so they seek to spend their whole life meditating on this divine love, saying with the tongue of the Church:

1.1.1.en: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine. Because of the savour of thy good ointments thy name is as ointment poured forth, therefore do the virgins love thee” [2-3].

1.1.2.en: This is the voice of the universal Church, having lifted her eyes to the Cross, so that she smelled its sweet fragrance and saw His name poured forth for her sake, and found delight in His love; therefore she began to converse with Him, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” Here we observe the following: 1. She asks for the kisses of the mouth of the Father. “Let him kiss me” (He Himself). Truly God has kissed her with many kisses through the ages. He declared His love for her, so He created the whole world for her sake, brought her into being out of nothing, and gave her His image and likeness; in short, she lacked nothing. After the fall He did not abandon her but promised her salvation, granted her the written Law as a help, and sent the prophets to confirm His salvation to her... But all this will not satisfy the bride, for she wants Him Himself to draw near to her and give her Himself... She wants all the kisses of His direct mouth! It is as though she were a bride who rejoices in the bridegroom who asks for her hand and sends his relatives to her, and keeps sending her precious gifts... but she is not satisfied; rather she asks for him himself!

1.1.3.en: In this Origen says: [The Church in the Old Testament was like a young girl, not yet mature; she did not enjoy the company of the Bridegroom Himself directly, but enjoyed the company of His friends, that is, the angels, the Fathers and the prophets, and through them she received the kisses of God, which are the teaching of the New Testament and its commandments. She was on the way of growth, moving toward maturity to see her Bridegroom coming to her upon the mountains of the Law and the hills of the prophecies, and her heart was set ablaze with love for Him, saying: “Let Him come and descend to me and kiss me Himself on the Cross, to embrace me with practical love that I may be united with Him.” This is what the Apostle Paul declared in his speech to the Hebrews when he says: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son” (Heb 1:1-2)... He spoke to us with the kisses of direct, practical love. 2. She is not ashamed to ask the Son for the kisses of the Father, because what belongs to the Father belongs to the Son also. And what the Son offered by His will He offered in obedience to the Father. For this reason Scripture affirms: “For God (the Father) so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son” (Jn 3:16), and at the same time the Apostle says, “who loved me, and gave himself for me”... The kisses of the Cross for us are a sign of the love of the Father and of the Son as well!].

1.1.4.en: We have already seen that this expression cannot apply to any bodily, temporal love, since the bride would be asking her bridegroom for the kisses of another than himself; but the talk here is of the divine, spiritual kisses that carry the meaning of the hidden union, that we may be one with the Father in His Son through the kisses of the Cross. 3. The bride does not ask for a kiss or two or more, but wants all “the kisses of his mouth”... These are the feelings of the believer when his heart opens to the love of God: he sees as though there were nothing in life but God and himself, and so he asks for all of God’s love for him. 4. The Church does not ask only for all the kisses of the Lord, but she asks for a special kind of kisses, namely “the kisses of his mouth,” which express the firm and unique marital relationship in which no other shares with the two of them.

1.1.5.en: Holy Scripture has recorded for us different kinds of kisses, but they are not satisfying kisses. Laban bade farewell to his sons and daughters with kisses (Gen 31:55); Jacob received his two grandsons, the sons of Joseph, with kisses (Gen 48:10); Naomi bade farewell to her two daughters-in-law with weeping and kissing (Ruth 1:9); Isaac asked his son Jacob to come near and kiss him so that he might receive a blessing (Gen 27:26); Absalom the son of David came forward to kiss the people so as to win their hearts (2 Sam 15:5); Jonathan kissed David the prophet as a sign of friendship and a covenant of loyalty (1 Sam 20:41); and the church of Ephesus bade farewell to the Apostle Paul with weeping and kissing (Acts 20:37). All these were kisses that took place because of a bond of blood, or kinship, or friendship, or as a sign of the pains of parting... but they are temporary kisses, whereas the Church asks for the kisses of eternal love, the kisses of the mouth of God that never cease.

1.2.0.en: The Church addresses her Bridegroom who was crucified for her sake, saying: “For thy love is better than wine.” It is a love that makes the soul drunk, so that she forgets everything earthly and wanders in the love of God alone.

1.2.1.en: The word “thy love” came in the Septuagint as “thy breasts,” as though the believers find in the divine milk flowing from the two breasts, which satisfies little children, a sweetness, effectiveness and power greater than that of the wine that men use for warmth and strength. In this St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [What is lofty in the wisdom of the world becomes very small before the teachings that we receive from the divine Word presented to children. Here we find the divine breasts better than human wine].

1.2.2.en: When the soul repeats, “Thy breasts are better than wine,” she returns to the simplicity of childhood; she looks to her betrothed lifted up on the Cross and clings to Him in the simplicity of faith, like a child on its mother’s breast... She nurses from the two breasts of the love of God, so she forgets all the cares of life and is filled with consolation, as the psalmist says: “In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul” (Ps 94:19).

1.2.3.en: “Thy breasts are better than wine”... Wine used to be offered to guests, especially at feasts, as a sign of joy, and was also offered with sacrifices (Ex 29:40; Lev 23:13; Num 15:5); but the love of the Lord Christ is unique, giving a joy that the world cannot take away!

1.2.4.en: Grapes in Egypt, and perhaps in Palestine, were pressed by being crushed with the feet in the winepress (Neh 13:15; Job 14:11), so that the juice (blood) of the red grapes flowed, and the men came out with their garments reddened. But the prophet Isaiah saw the Lord Christ—the loving Bridegroom—great in power, glorious, passing through the winepress in reddened garments for the salvation of His bride... and he asked, saying:

1.2.5.en: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?

1.2.6.en: this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength?

1.2.7.en: I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.

1.2.8.en: Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?

1.2.9.en: I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” (Isa 63:1-4).

1.2.10.en: This is the unique love, better than wine... The Lord passed through the winepress alone, not to offer earthly wine but to offer His blood poured out for us, the mystery of our life, our strength and our salvation.

1.2.11.en: No wonder that the Lord began His ministry at the wedding of Cana of Galilee, turning water into wine, not that they might become drunk but rather that they might be sobered from drunkenness; He gave them the new wine as a sign of His love, the Giver of joy and strength. In this St. John Chrysostom says: [At that time, and now also, He does not cease to change our weakness and our feeble will. Yes, for there are people who differ in nothing from water: cold and weak and full of fluidity (slackness). Let us bring such people into the presence of the Lord that He may change their will into wine, so that they are no longer like flowing water but become firm, and become a mystery of joy to their own souls and to others]. This is the love better than wine, which brings our weak nature into the new life so that it carries the power of life.

1.2.12.en: Through this new wine, or through the love of the Bridegroom, better than wine, the believing soul smells the sweet fragrance of the ointments of Christ and sees His name as ointment poured forth, since He passed through the Cross alone. She addresses Him, saying:

1.2.13.en: “Because of the savour of thy good ointments thy name is as ointment poured forth” [2].

1.3.s.en: The one anointed with the sweet ointment:

1.3.0.en: On the Cross the Lord poured out the perfection of His love, so He spread His sweet fragrance in the whole world, and His name appeared in all the earth.

1.3.1.en: A sweet fragrance spread, and the Church realized that He is the very One anointed by the Father for our salvation, to whom the prophet bore witness: “Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows” (Ps 44; Heb 1:9). Indeed the Lord affirmed this when He entered the synagogue as His custom was and opened the book of the prophet Isaiah and said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised...” Then He began to say to them that this day this Scripture was fulfilled in their ears (Lk 4:17-21; Isa 61:1).

1.3.2.en: And when the Jews rose in tumult against the Apostles, the Church prayed thus: “Of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together” (Acts 4:27).

1.3.3.en: In the Old Testament, Jacob anointed the stone that had been under his head and set it up as a pillar in the house of the Lord (Gen 28:18; 31:13), as a sign of heaven being opened to the earth, or the meeting between God and man, or God’s dwelling in the midst of His people. According to the Law, the priests were anointed (Ex 40:15), likewise the kings (1 Sam 10:1), and the Temple and everything within it and the vessels of the house of God were anointed with a holy anointing. This anointing, whether of persons or of things, means their consecration to the Lord, so that persons do not practice other works in the world besides the service of the Lord, and the Temple or the holy vessels are not used for any purpose other than the service of the Lord. And when we speak of “the service of the Lord” we mean “the service of the Lord in the midst of His people,” or bringing man into the presence of the Lord, that is, the service of the Lord through humanity and not in isolation from them. Therefore when we speak of the Bridegroom, “the Word of God,” as the Anointed One, we see in Him the fulfillment of the anointing in its most perfect form, for He carried us in Himself and brought us into union with God... This is the work of the Savior, for He says, “For their sakes I sanctify myself (that is, He consecrated His work for us)... that they also might be sanctified through the truth.”

1.3.4.en: This unique anointing has had its fragrance spread in heaven, for the Father smelled it as a fragrance of good pleasure, since it carried the fragrance of the obedience of the beloved only-begotten Son who obeyed unto death; and we also on earth smell it as a sweet fragrance, since it kills the stench of our sins (Ps 83:5) and makes of us “a sweet savour” (2 Cor 2:15). This is the effectiveness of His anointing, that He is the Christ who makes of sinners anointed ones who have His sweet fragrance.

1.3.5.en: The Fathers of the Church have spoken of the effects of this holy anointing in our lives. St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees in the mystery of Baptism... that the baptized person enjoys the characteristics of Christ, so that the sweet fragrance of Christ wafts in all his senses, for he says: [Let us be healed in the sense of smell also... so that dust may not rise upon us but the sweet fragrance (Isa 5:24); let us smell the ointment poured out for us, let us receive it in us spiritually, so that we are formed and changed by it, and they smell in us the sweet fragrance].

1.3.6.en: And St. Augustine sees that the good ointments are the fragrance of the heavenly Christ, who draws the heart by His Cross to heaven, for he says:

1.3.7.en: [Let us love Him and imitate Him, let us run after His ointments...

1.3.8.en: He has come and spread His sweet fragrance, which filled the world!

1.3.9.en: From where did this sweet fragrance come? From heaven!].

1.3.10.en: Therefore, walk toward heaven if you wish not to answer in vain when it is said to you: Lift up your hearts... lift up your thoughts, lift up your love and your hope, lest these things be corrupted on earth... for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Mt 6:21).

1.3.11.en: St. Augustine also speaks of the attraction of this sweet ointment, saying: [Let us turn our senses away from our foul odor and turn toward Him, that we may catch our breath a little!]

1.4.0.en: On the Cross He poured out this sweet ointment, and entered the tomb with it so that the dead might breathe the fragrance of the ointment instead of the corruption that had befallen them, and by His Resurrection He offered to the world this sweet ointment poured forth.

1.4.1.en: St. Ambrose says: [This is what the believer experiences, buried with Christ in Baptism and rising, so that he smells the fragrance of the garments of the Lord, and breathes His name poured forth on the Cross, and drinks in the fragrance of the Resurrection].

1.4.2.en: And the wonder is that this sweet name, when it was poured forth on the Cross, spread its fragrance in the whole world, so that the name of God was no longer known among the Jews alone as it had been before, but the nations and peoples of the world came to know Him. In this St. Ambrose says: [God was known in Judah and His name was great in Israel (Ps 26:1); but now that He has been lifted up on the Cross, His name has become wonderful in all the earth].

1.4.3.en: In other words, on the Cross humanity came to know His name, that He is “Jesus,” the Savior of men, and that He is Immanuel (God with us). For through the Cross we realized His salvation and understood? [His] being with us in our reconciliation with God; therefore we address Him, saying: “Thy name is as ointment poured forth.”

1.5.s.en: The love of the virgins for Him:

1.5.0.en: When humanity smelled the fragrance of His name poured forth, it was drawn to Him with virginal hearts that do not want to be occupied with another besides Him, and its thoughts flowed toward Him in a virginity that does not want to think of the concerns of life or its enticements, and its feelings and emotions and all its inner energies were released toward Him... saying: “Therefore do the virgins love thee” [3].

1.5.1.en: This attraction that the Cross created in our inner depths, until everything within us went out as virgins seeking the Bridegroom alone, gives birth to an attraction in us, so that we do not run to Him alone, but draw with us many who run to Him with joy; therefore the human soul addresses Him, saying:

1.5.2.en: “Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine.

1.5.4.en: She says: “Draw me (I), and we will run (we) after thee; I will enter (I) into thy chambers, and we will be glad (we) and rejoice (we) in thee...”.

1.5.5.en: This is the mystery of the Cross and its effectiveness: it carries the power of witness and attraction, and the mystery of gladness and joy!

1.5.6.en: When my soul enjoys You, and You are within me through the Cross, and I become in You, people come to know You through me and seek You; then our hearts are filled with gladness and joy, even the heavenly ones rejoice with us!

1.5.7.en: Zacchaeus the tax collector was drawn after the Lord Christ, so he gathered sinners and tax collectors to meet the Lord and rejoice in Him; and when the Samaritan woman sat with Him, she called the people of the city to sit with Him and enjoy His effective speech.

1.5.8.en: This is the mystery of the Church... the attractive power of the Cross. But if the Church forgets this Cross and busies herself with the ways of the world, she cannot outdo the world in what belongs to it; rather she overcomes it by love through the Cross at work in the lives of her children.

1.5.9.en: By the Cross alone souls are drawn to the Church through repentance, whereas the enticing means of the world shatter the image of the Church even in the eyes of the world itself.

1.6.0.en: “The king hath brought me into his chambers” [4].

1.6.1.en: The soul asked for the hand of the heavenly Bridegroom, saying, “Draw me,” that He might support her and hold her and bring her into His spiritual chambers in the most joyous meeting.

1.6.2.en: Origen sees the soul in a state of being drawn and entering into the chambers of the Lord as an image of spiritual believers whose minds have been released from the literal interpretation of the word of God and, by the power of the Holy Spirit, have entered into the mysteries of the Word, or the deep spiritual interpretation; she enters to the Bridegroom Himself and discovers the mysteries of His kingdom. This is the divine chamber... which is the spiritual interpretation of the Word, which satisfies the soul not only in this life but in eternity also, or, as Origen sees it, is the heavenly food of the soul.

1.6.3.en: Some Fathers see that “the divine chamber” is “the mystery of Baptism.” For in the baptismal font the believer meets the Lord Christ as his Bridegroom. He puts on the new man and enjoys the divine Kingdom. The soul puts on her Christ as a white garment for the eternal wedding, putting Him on as righteousness for herself, for the mystery of her holiness; she is adorned by Him, and lives by Him forever. In this the Apostle Paul says: “have put on Christ” (Gal 3:27).

1.7.0.en: When the soul puts on her Christ as righteousness for her and sanctification of her life, she compares her past with her present, and addresses the daughters of Jerusalem thus: “I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon” [5]. She confesses her own weakness but declares her beauty, which she acquired through her union with Christ Jesus her Lord, saying: “I am black as the tents of Kedar,” which have no beauty, but at the same time I am beautiful like the curtains of Solomon (or, as it came in the Latin translation, like the curtains of Salma).

1.7.1.en: St. Augustine sees the human soul before its union with the Lord as a piece of black coal, but when she is united with Him she is set ablaze by His holy fire, her blackness vanishes and she becomes burning coals of fire, hot in spirit, full of beauty. St. Augustine offered Saul of Tarsus as an example, saying: [The Apostle was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and an injurer; he was black coal, not kindled; but when he received mercy he was set ablaze with fire from heaven. The voice of Christ set him on fire and removed all blackness from him; he became ablaze with the heat of the Spirit, so that he kindled others with the same fire that burned in him].

1.7.2.en: St. Ambrose sees in this expression an image of the state of the Church, who enjoyed spiritual beauty and by faith was perfected in the baptismal font by the grace of God, for he says: [Having put on those garments through the baptismal font, she says in the Song of Songs: I am black and comely (perfect), O daughters of Jerusalem. I am black through human weakness, perfect through the mystery of faith!].

1.7.3.en: He also says: [The Church is black by her sins, perfect by grace. She is black by human nature, perfect by salvation... black with the dust of the struggle, perfect when she is crowned with the ornaments of victory!].

1.7.4.en: This expression is in truth a medicine for the believer: when he feels his own righteousness and is fought by pride, he cries out in his depths, “I am black,” and if his soul is weighed down by weakness and fought by faintheartedness or despair, he repeats with power, “I am beautiful.” As though the two feelings of “blackness and beauty” are not contradictory but each completes the other. One feeling supports in some moments and the other supports in other moments. The two feelings lead to a state of balance within the soul: the feeling of one’s own weakness together with an awareness of the power of the work of divine grace.

1.7.5.en: Origen has a beautiful interpretation of this expression... saying:

1.7.6.en: [The Church here directs her speech—not to the Bridegroom, nor to the virgins who go about on the way—but to the daughters of Jerusalem, who accused the Church the bride of ugliness and made a spectacle of her blackness; so the Church answers this accusation with a speech in which she affirms the truth of the accusation, because she is indeed black, and thus appears as the daughters of Jerusalem judged her. But if only the daughters of Jerusalem would perceive the inner beauty of the Church, for while she is black she is beautiful.

1.7.7.en: Although she is in the blackness and ugliness of Kedar, yet she is in the beauty of the hangings—that is, the curtains—of the house of King Solomon.

1.7.8.en: The Church who speaks this speech is the Church of the multitudes of the Gentiles... And of what can the Church of the Gentiles boast before the earthly daughters of Jerusalem, that is, the Jews? Who poured out the full cup of their wrath upon the Church and her Bridegroom, and heaped upon the Church every contempt and scorn, and attributed to her lowliness and meanness of origin, because there does not run in the veins of her members and children the blood of descent from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob... This is the great offense in the eyes of the Jews, that the Church of the Gentiles is not of the seed of the Fathers. And the Church confesses this, and repeats the same accusation with which she was reproached by the daughters of Jerusalem, “I am black,” and this blackness is not only the deprivation of the descent of the Fathers, but also the deprivation of the teaching of the Fathers and the prophets.

1.7.9.en: Those whom the Law rejected and who were driven out from the tent of Isaac, the Gospel has clothed with the beauty of the hangings and curtains of the house of King Solomon... And what are the curtains of the house of the king of peace but the curtains of the tabernacle of meeting where God dwells with His people... the tabernacle that was covered on the outside with unlovely goats’ skins... and contained on the inside the splendor of the curtains, besides the glory of God in it... The curtains of the tabernacle are... on the outside goats’ hair and rams’ skins dyed red and badgers’ skins, while on the inside the curtains are of blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen].

1.7.10.en: Origen presented some events and expressions of the Old Testament that foretold the calling of the community of the black Gentiles and their entry into union with Christ as a beautiful and holy bride for Him, namely: 1. The marriage of Moses the prophet to the Cushite woman (dark of skin), a matter that stirred up his sister, so she spoke against him and made a spectacle of him (Num 12); therefore she was struck with leprosy and put outside the camp. This act bore a symbolic picture of the union of the Lord Christ with the Church of the Gentiles, a matter that stirred up the Jews so that they refused to believe in Him, and they went on reproaching the Gentiles with their evil past.

1.7.11.en: Origen speaks on the tongue of the Church of the Gentiles as she addresses the Jews, saying: [Truly I marvel, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you rebuke me for the blackness of my skin. Have you forgotten what is in your Law and what Miriam meant when she spoke against Moses because he had taken to himself a black Cushite woman?! And do you not know that this type has truly been fulfilled in me?! I am the Cushite! Truly I am black because of the baseness of my origin, but I am beautiful through repentance and faith. I have taken to myself the Son of God. I have received “the Word who was made flesh” (Jn 1:14), I have come to Him who is “the image of God... the firstborn of every creature” (Col 1:15), “who is the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3), so I became beautiful! What are you doing? Do you rebuke one who has left her sin, a thing which the Law forbids?! Do you seek the glory of the Law while you violate it?!]. 2. The story of the queen of Sheba who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kgs 10), which bore a type of the Church of the Gentiles, for she came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kgs 10), to which the Lord Himself pointed, rebuking the Jews, saying: “The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here” (Mt 12:42).

1.7.12.en: The queen of Sheba came and communed with him of all that was in her heart (1 Kgs 10:2) and tested him with questions and riddles she thought had no answer, but the true Solomon solved all her problems, and declared to her the knowledge of the true God, and explained to her the immortality of the soul and the final judgment... matters that the philosophers were unable to explain truly to the Gentiles.

1.7.13.en: The queen came to “Jerusalem,” which means “vision of peace,” and the Lord Christ in the week of His passion declared to the Church His capacities, saying: “My peace I give unto you.”

1.7.14.en: When the queen saw what belonged to Solomon “there was no more spirit in her” (1 Kgs 10:5); and the Church, as she discovers the mysteries of her suffering Christ, melts with love and can no longer do anything but go forth and be with Him.

1.7.15.en: She presented to King Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold (1 Kgs 10:10), which is the same number the Lord allowed in the days of Noah for the age of man (Gen 6:3), and is the age of Moses the prophet (Deut 34:7), as though the Church of the Gentiles wanted to offer all her age as golden talents, that is, to carry the heavenly nature.

1.7.16.en: She also presented much spice (1 Kgs 10:10), which is the offering of love that the Lord Christ receives from repentant sinners. 3. In the book of Psalms it is said: “Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God. Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto the Lord” (Ps 68:31-32). Thus the Church of the black Gentiles (Cush) stretches out her hands to God and becomes beautiful, and through her the tongue of all the kingdoms of the earth is released in praising Him. 4. It is written in Zephaniah: “Therefore wait ye upon me, saith the LORD... For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent... From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia my suppliants, even my dispersed, shall bring mine offering” (Song 3:8-10). Thus the pagan peoples are turned into pure lips of praise, and cross the rivers of Cush, that is, leave their blackness and darkness through their worship of God and the offering of the sacrifice of Christ. 5. When the Cushite king rescued Jeremiah and brought him up with ropes from the pit (Jer 38:7-13), the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah: “Go and speak to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring my words upon this city for evil... But I will deliver thee in that day, saith the LORD: and thou shalt not be given into the hand of the men of whom thou art afraid. For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD” (Jer 39:15-18). Thus this Cushite man was a type of the Church of the black Gentiles who trusted in God, and He saved her.

1.7.17.en: Origen concluded this comparison of his by saying: [There are many expressions—as you see—that bear witness to this black and comely woman who behaves well toward the daughters of Jerusalem, and affirms with confidence: Truly I am dark (black) as the tents of Kedar, but I am comely as the curtains of Solomon].

1.7.18.en: Origen has another remark: [Although the speaker appears to be one person, she likens herself to tents and curtains in the plural; therefore we need to know that the speaker here is a community of countless churches spread in the world and gatherings of peoples, just as it is said of the Kingdom of God that it is one, and yet it mentions many mansions in the Father’s house (Jn 14:2)].

1.8.s.en: Between the sun of trials and the Sun of Righteousness:

1.8.0.en: The bride gives a reason for her blackness or darkness, saying:

1.8.1.en: “Look not upon me, because I am black (dark in color), because the sun hath looked upon me” [6].

1.8.2.en: It was fitting for the Jews to support the Gentiles and preach the Cross to them, but instead of preaching they stood reproaching them with the blackness that had befallen them because of idolatry; but the Gentiles answered that their blackness is not natural, something they were molded in, but is the result of what they suffered when they “went down” under the sun and it scorched them. Origen comments on this saying: [She became black because she went down, but as soon as she began to rise, “coming up from the wilderness” (Song 8:5), leaning upon her sister’s son (who came born of the community of the Jews), allowing nothing to separate her from him, she becomes white and beautiful. For her blackness is completely dispelled and she shines with the rays of the light that surrounds her. Thus she (the Church of the Gentiles) apologizes to the daughters of Jerusalem for her blackness, saying: Do not suppose, O daughters of Jerusalem, that the blackness imprinted on my face is natural, but understand that it happened because the Sun of Righteousness ignored me. For the “Sun of Righteousness” did not direct His rays upon me directly, because He found me not upright. I am the people of the Gentiles, who did not look to the Sun of Righteousness, nor did I stand before the Lord (Lk 21:36)... For since I did not believe in the old time, God chose you and you obtained mercy and the “Sun of Righteousness” cared for you, while He ignored me and scorched me because of my disobedience and unbelief. But now that you have become unbelieving and disobedient, I have hope that the “Sun of Righteousness” will look upon me, and I shall find mercy!].

1.8.3.en: Perhaps this clarifies the saying of the Apostle Paul: “that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in... For as ye in times past have not believed God, yet have now obtained mercy through their unbelief” (Rom 11:25, 30). In ancient times the Gentiles were burdened by the sun of trials, deprived of the Sun of Righteousness, so Israel was given the opportunity to be chosen and shown mercy; but now that the Jews have rejected the Sun of Righteousness and fallen under the sun of disobedience and unbelief, the Church of the Gentiles has enjoyed Christ the Sun of Righteousness. Her old blackness has vanished by the shining of the Sun of Righteousness upon her! And the sun of sin no longer has power over her, as the psalmist says: “The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps 120:6).

1.9.0.en: When the Church met her suffering Bridegroom, He drew her to Himself, so she entered His chambers and rejoiced in Him; He quenched her thirst with His infinite love, so His sweet fragrance spread, sanctifying all her depths and feelings, removing from her the darkness of sin and the blackness of evil, reflecting His beauty upon her; therefore the powers of darkness can do nothing but rise up against the bride.

1.9.2.en: “My mother’s children were angry with me; they made me the keeper (guardian) of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept” [6].

1.9.3.en: Who are the sons of her mother? And what is the secret of their anger against her?

1.9.4.en: And what is the vineyard that the bride keeps, and her own vineyard that she does not keep? 1. Origen sees that the accurate translation of the text is: “My mother’s children fought in me” and not against me. Here “the sons of her mother” are the Apostles who are of the community of the Jews, since the Gentiles and the Jews are of one mother. These Apostles did not cease to stir up a violent war within the Gentiles until they pulled down all the towers of falsehood and shattered the strongholds of the erroneous pagan teachings and overcame all evil, so that they might raise up from the pagan Gentiles “a keeper of the vineyard of the Lord” and a preserver of the Law and the prophets, while her “own vineyard,” that is, her pagan teachings, she no longer keeps or cares for. 2. Origen has another opinion, which is that the angels are “the sons of her mother,” for men and angels have become belonging to one mother, all have become members in the Church of Christ. These angels support us and fight for us and with us, as the Lord sends them to our help in the inner war against sin, so that the soul may be able to tend the vineyard of the Lord which is “the heart” and abandon her own vineyard or the works of her old man, so that she no longer keeps them but gives them up. 3. There is a third interpretation, which is that “the sons of the mother” refers to “the ego” or “the self,” for “a man’s foes shall be they of his own household” (Mt 10:36). The human self is an enemy that rises up against the work of Christ in us. During this war the believer cares for the vineyards of others and is occupied in pride with the outward show of service and preaching without caring for his inner vineyard or his inner life.

1.10.0.en: When the Church spoke of her Bridegroom “the suffering Messiah,” and saw in His sufferings an attraction so that many were drawn with her to Him, the enemy rose up against her... Therefore the Church cries out to the same Bridegroom as “the Good Shepherd,” who enters into her life and shepherds her Himself; she addresses Him, saying:

1.10.1.en: “Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest down at noon?” [7].

1.10.2.en: In the midst of the bitterness of her heart because of the severity of the enemy’s war against her, the human soul feels the sweetness of the care of God her Shepherd, so she calls Him “O thou whom my soul loveth.” It is as though she says with St. Gregory of Nyssa: [This is the name by which I call You (O thou whom my soul loveth), for Your name is above all things, and is incomprehensible even to all rational creatures. This name proclaims Your goodness, and draws my soul to You. How can I not love You, who loved me thus while I was black (Song 1:4), and laid down Your life for the flock which is the object of Your care?!].

1.11.0.en: She asks the Shepherd, whom she loved with all her heart and soul, about the place of His rest, that she may rest with Him and in Him... She asks Him the way so that she may not walk according to her own personal desires.

1.11.1.en: In ancient times when the sun of trials grew intense upon the prophet David, he took refuge in the house of God as the place where God feeds and lies down at noon, for he said:

1.11.2.en: “Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident.

1.11.3.en: One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple. For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock.

1.11.4.en: And now shall mine head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me: therefore will I offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto the LORD”

1.11.6.en: Truly, how much we need the Shepherd Himself to take us by the hand and bring us into His Church, the place of His rest, the pasture of salvation... There we meet the Lord Christ Himself, the mystery of our rest and peace, and enjoy the gifts of His Holy Spirit who comforts us. In His house we received sonship to God through Baptism, and received His Holy Spirit dwelling in us through the sacrament of the Holy Myron. In His house we find the forgiveness of sins and are refreshed by the life-giving Sacrifice, the Body and Blood of the Son of God given for us... In His house we sit under the shadow of His Cross, the mystery of our reconciliation with God and our inner peace. When the enemy intensifies the war against us, and when sin rises up within us, we run to His house with tears of repentance and find the Shepherd Himself searching for us, and His Holy Spirit longing for our sanctification!

1.12.0.en: Why did the bride choose to meet her Bridegroom the Shepherd at noon, saying, “where thou liest down at noon?”

1.12.1.en: If we meet the Good Shepherd in His one Church, extending through the ages, she enters into Him that we may see Him transfigured in her like the noonday sun... so that her members know neither darkness nor shadows, but live continually at the zenith of the light of their Shepherd, enlightened by Him and so becoming in their turn light to the world. In this the wise man says: “But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. The way of the wicked is as darkness” (Prov 4:18-19).

1.12.2.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [You make me lie down at noon... in the light that knows no shadow, for no shadow is found at noon when the sun is perpendicular to us].

1.12.3.en: No one can be qualified for the rest of noon unless he is a son of the day and of the light... The bride says: “Show me how I may lie down? Make known to me the way of the rest of noon, lest I stray from Your faithful leadership, and ignorance of the truth befall me, a thing that befalls the flocks opposed to Your flock!”.

1.12.4.en: And St. Augustine says: [What does noon mean? Intense heat and great brightness! Then I recognize You, whose wise ones are fervent in spirit, shining in teaching].

1.12.5.en: Origen sees in noon a symbol of the perfection of God’s splendor; the bride wants to cleave to the Lord in the fullness of His majesty, as she addresses Him thus, saying: “It is sweet to me to seek You at this very time, for in seeking You I find no evening, nor when You feed in the morning, nor at sunset; rather I seek You at this time... in the middle of the day when You are in the fullness of Your light... in the brightness of Your majesty!”.

1.12.6.en: Origen has another interpretation of the word “noon,” namely the perception of the perfection of knowing the mysteries of the word of God, for he says: [What you call noon refers to the hidden places of the heart, where the soul follows the trace of the light of the knowledge of the word of God that is clearer, because noon is the time when the sun is at its zenith. Therefore when the Lord Christ—the Sun of Righteousness—shows the mysteries of His lofty and sublime power to His Church, He makes known to her the places of His joyful pastures and the places of His rest at noon. The Church at the beginning, as she learns the “elementary” things, receives from Him the rays of hidden knowledge, so the prophet says: “God shall help her, and that right early” (Ps 45:6); but now that she seeks the more perfect things and we long for loftier things, she asks for the light of the knowledge of noon].

1.13.s.en: A meeting with the Shepherd at noon:

1.13.0.en: The Church wants to meet her Bridegroom at noon, because this time has effective memories in her life; we mention by way of example: 1. At noon the Lord appeared to Abraham with two angels, and announced to him and Sarah his wife that He would raise up for them offspring who would be a blessing to many nations (Gen 18)... He raises up for them from the womb of Sarah, which was as good as dead, and from Abraham’s old age, a new life. This is what the Church asks of her Shepherd at noon, that she may meet Him surrounded by His angels, and enter with Him into the fellowship of heavenly glories, that He may give her her inner Isaac, that is, give her “the new life”; He raises up in us this life in spite of what we were in... we are under the sentence of death and fruitless, and as Abraham and Sarah experienced “the power of the resurrection,” as the Lord raised up life for them from their death, so we ask our Shepherd that we may experience continually the power of the resurrection in us.

1.13.1.en: As Abraham the father of fathers met God at noon outside the tent, so the children of Abraham who do the works of Abraham (Jn 8:39) are bound to go outside the limits of the temporary tent of the body, driving out from themselves by the Holy Spirit every carnal thought and carnal lust, so that they may enjoy the vision of God and the enjoyment of His care. 2. And at noon Joseph met his younger brother Benjamin, and his bowels yearned upon him, and he could not but enter his chamber and weep (Gen 43). This is the picture of the meeting that we desire, where the true firstborn Shepherd Jesus Christ meets us, His younger brothers, sees us and His bowels yearn upon us, and calls us “Benjamin,” that is, “sons of the right hand.” 3. At noon Elijah mocked the priests of Baal, saying: “Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked” (1 Kgs 18:27); thus the Church wants to draw near to her Shepherd at noon to see Him as the true Elijah, that is, “my God,” who mocks the devil and all his hosts... And this was fulfilled when the Messiah was lifted up on the Cross at noon to crush Satan and all his hosts, giving us authority to tread him under our feet. 4. At noon the true Shepherd Jesus Christ revealed Himself to Saul of Tarsus, who had devoted his energies to the destruction of the name of Jesus (Acts 22:9), and Saul discovered the truth of the living Shepherd who does not die, and his life was transformed into a chosen vessel bearing witness to the name of Jesus Christ among many nations. This is the shepherding of the Messiah, to turn persecutors into preachers and servants of the Word. 5. Finally, the bride’s expression “where thou liest down at noon” recalls the prophecy of our father Jacob to Judah, saying: “Judah is a lion’s whelp... he stooped down, he couched as a lion... who shall rouse him up? The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be” (Gen 49:9-10). This prophecy was fulfilled when the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah couched and slept on the Cross at the sixth hour, not to rest but to shepherd humanity in love, offering His blood as a ransom and salvation.

1.14.0.en: The Church asks her Shepherd: “Where dost thou feed? Where dost thou lie down...? Lest I be as one light and veiled beside the flocks of thy companions?” [7].

1.14.1.en: Origen comments on this expression thus: [She longs to learn the way in which she must walk, lest, through not knowing its turnings, she turn aside to the flocks of His companions... and many others see her besides Him. As though she says: I want no one to see me but You alone. I wish to know the way that brings me to You... and that no one come between us].

1.14.2.en: She wants to know the true way so as to enjoy the shepherding of Christ, lest she become “light,” shaken by the winds of strange teachings, and be cast among the flocks of shepherds who work for their own account and not for the account of the Lord Christ. Thus she becomes “veiled,” her face hidden behind the veil instead of meeting her Shepherd with unveiled face; in other words she is deprived of being the bride united with her Bridegroom without any veil separating them.

1.14.3.en: St. Jerome sees that the veil here refers to “the veil of the old Law,” for when the bride meets her Shepherd at the Cross at noon she no longer wears a veil, since the curtain was torn and the era of shadows ended, and we entered a new covenant in which we meet God with unveiled face, that is, with the boldness of filial love or marital love. We no longer need a veil that we put over our face like Moses, but we enter into the mysteries of God and are in His presence united with Him.

1.15.0.en: The Shepherd answers His Church thus:

1.15.1.en: “If thou know not (thyself), O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents” [8].

1.15.2.en: Since she asked Him about His own way so as not to become light and veiled, turning aside to the flocks of the companions, the Shepherd made clear to her the features of the way in three points: 1. She first comes to know herself, and perceives the new nature that was given to her through His shepherding. 2. She goes out of isolation and self-centeredness, imitating the holy Fathers. 3. She bears witness to the Shepherd before the kids so as to bring them into the place of His shepherding. 1. The Good Shepherd first asks her to know herself, that is, to begin with the inside, to realize that God created her in His image and likeness without blemish, and adorned her with the unique beauty, “the fairest among women,” and paid the price in shepherding her through the Cross.
